# Venture Capital and the Capital Chokepoint {#sec-4-05}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1957–1980
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does access to money become a monopoly?

**The answer.** By making a road the only door. Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia both
open in 1972, both on Sand Hill Road, both minutes from Stanford. Venture
capital is not principally investment; it is gatekeeping. To scale, a company
must pass through a small physical corridor and a tight social network — which
is precisely what the Southern Pacific required of freight a century earlier.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control of the input that everything else depends
on. Geography encodes it: money, talent, and legitimacy inside a two-mile
radius. The chapter's job is to make the reader see Sand Hill Road as a toll
gate.

**The key fact.** Both Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital were founded in 1972,
and both located on Sand Hill Road. The capital corridor and the university sit
within walking distance of one another, and the adjacency is not coincidental —
it is the product.

**The human anchor.** Sand Hill Road itself: an unremarkable suburban road with
low buildings and a view of the foothills, through which a large share of the
world's consequential technology funding has passed.

**Excluded voices.** Everyone outside the network, and the chapter must be
specific rather than gestural: who did not get funded, and the documented
demographics of founders who did. Also the pension-fund beneficiaries whose
capital this is, and who have no say in its deployment — the 1979 ERISA
reinterpretation is what let it in.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that access to capital became a chokepoint by
showing funding concentrate in a small number of firms in a single physical
corridor adjacent to one university.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Sand Hill Road is an unremarkable suburban road in Menlo Park with low
buildings, parking lots, oak trees, and a view of the foothills. A very large
share of the world's consequential technology funding has passed through it, and
the chapter begins by describing it as a place before saying what it is.

What it is, is a toll gate. Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital were both
founded in 1972, both on that road, both minutes from Stanford, and their
founders came out of the industry rather than out of finance. Venture capital is
described as investment and functions as gatekeeping: a term sheet controls not
only money but hiring, customers, the next round, and the exit. To scale, a
company had to pass through a small physical corridor and a tight social
network, which is precisely what the Southern Pacific required of freight a
century earlier.

The chapter explains why the form was necessary. A semiconductor startup in 1957
had no collateral, no revenue, and enormous variance, which made it unfundable
by a bank. Arthur Rock's equity model from chapter 3 solved that, and the 1972
firms industrialised it.

The public-money leg is the part the drafts omitted and the chapter restores. In
1979 the Department of Labor clarified the prudent man rule under ERISA in a way
that permitted pension funds to invest in venture capital, and the scale of
available capital changed by an order of magnitude within a few years. The
retirement savings of American workers became the raw material of the Valley's
capital chokepoint, and those workers have no say in its deployment.

Proximity matters because the asset being traded is judgement about people,
which does not travel well. Geographic concentration is a feature of the
mechanism, not an accident of it.

The chapter closes on who is not funded, with sourced founder demographics
rather than gestures. The tightest chokepoint in the system is now four minutes
from the campus that supplies its deal flow.
:::

   it is four minutes from the campus that supplies its deal flow.

::: {.chapter-question}
How does access to money become a monopoly?
:::

Sand Hill Road runs west from the freeway at Menlo Park, past the Stanford
campus edge, and up into the foothills. It is a suburban road with low buildings
set back among oak trees, generous parking, and views toward the coastal range.
There is nothing to look at.

A very large share of the world's consequential technology funding over the last
fifty years has passed through those buildings, and the chapter's argument is
that this is a toll gate rather than a business district.

## Why a new form of capital was needed

Consider financing a semiconductor company in 1957.

It has no revenue. It has no collateral, because its assets are a lease, some
equipment, and eight men. It has enormous variance: it will either be worth a
great deal or nothing, with little in between. And nobody involved can say with
confidence what it will be worth, because the market it is entering does not yet
exist.

A bank cannot lend against that. A bank lends against assets and cash flow, at
interest, and requires the loan to be repaid whatever happens. Applied to a
startup, that structure destroys the company in the bad case and gives the
lender almost nothing in the good one.

Arthur Rock's insight in the Fairchild financing was to take equity instead. If
the enterprise fails, the money is gone. If it succeeds, the return is
unbounded. That asymmetry makes it rational to fund a portfolio of ventures most
of which will fail, and it is the entire mathematical basis of the industry that
follows.

Rock moved to San Francisco in 1961 and formed Davis and Rock, which funded
Scientific Data Systems and, in 1968, Intel. He was also explicit about what he
was actually assessing. He backed people rather than businesses, on the argument
that the plan would change and the founders would not.

## 1972

Two firms were founded in 1972, both on Sand Hill Road.

Kleiner Perkins was formed by Eugene Kleiner — one of the eight from chapter 2 —
and Tom Perkins, who had run Hewlett-Packard's computer division. Sequoia
Capital was founded by Don Valentine, who had been head of marketing at
Fairchild and then at National Semiconductor.

Note the provenance. These were not financiers who had moved into technology.
They were operators from the semiconductor industry who had moved into finance,
which meant they could evaluate technical claims and knew personally most of the
people worth funding. The capital and the industry were the same social network,
and they had been colleagues.

The physical clustering followed immediately, and it followed for a reason that
is not obvious until stated: the asset being traded is judgement about people,
and judgement about people does not travel. A partner needs to sit in the room,
know the founder's former manager, and hear what the market is saying this week.
Proximity to the deal flow — which meant proximity to Stanford — was the whole
business.

Four minutes from the campus that supplies the founders. That is the geography
of the chokepoint, and it has not moved.

## The public money leg

The industry's scale changed because of a regulatory clarification, and this is
the part that almost every account leaves out.

The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 imposed a prudent man
standard on pension fund investment, and fund managers read it as prohibiting
anything speculative. Venture capital, which was speculative by construction,
was effectively closed off from the largest pool of investable capital in the
country.

In 1979 the Department of Labor issued a clarification. The prudent man
standard, it said, applied to the portfolio as a whole rather than to each
investment in isolation, which meant a pension fund could allocate a small
percentage to high-variance assets without breaching its duty.

The effect was immediate and enormous. Capital committed to venture funds rose
by an order of magnitude over the following few years, and the dominant source
of it became pension money — the retirement savings of American workers,
institutional and public alike.

So the capital chokepoint runs on public and quasi-public money in exactly the
way the railroad did, and the beneficiaries of those pension funds have no say
in how it is deployed and mostly do not know it is being deployed this way. Act
III's triangle has acquired a fourth party.

## Gatekeeping, not investing

The chapter's central claim is that venture capital's function is selection
rather than finance, and the term sheet is the evidence.

Money is the smallest part of what a term sheet allocates. It sets the
valuation, which determines what the founders keep. It assigns board seats,
which determines who can remove them. It carries liquidation preferences, which
determine who is paid first if the company sells. It includes protective
provisions that give the investor a veto over the decisions that matter most:
raising more money, selling the company, changing the business.

Beyond the document, the firm supplies the things that actually determine the
outcome. Introductions to customers. Recruitment of executives. Credibility with
the next round of investors, which is nearly always the deciding factor.

A company that cannot get through Sand Hill Road does not merely lack money. It
lacks access to customers, executives, and subsequent capital, all of which are
routed through the same small number of partnerships.

The Southern Pacific decided which towns in the Central Valley would exist by
deciding where the line ran. Sand Hill Road decides which companies exist by
deciding which ones can scale. The mechanism is identical and the second version
attracts no regulatory attention whatsoever, because nobody has ever thought of
a venture fund as a common carrier.

## The other side of the corridor

Two further pieces completed the arrangement in the 1970s, and both are within a
few miles of the road.

The first is the law. A small number of Valley firms — Wilson Sonsini above all,
founded in Palo Alto in 1961 — developed a practice of representing startups on
terms adapted to companies with no money, sometimes taking equity in place of
fees. They standardised the documents. The consequence is that the terms on
which American technology companies are financed were substantially drafted by a
handful of firms within a few miles of Stanford, and the resulting templates are
now used everywhere.

The second is the bank. Silicon Valley Bank, founded in 1983, built a business
around lending to venture-backed companies and to the funds themselves, on
underwriting logic that no conventional bank used: it assessed the quality of
the investors behind a company rather than the company's own assets. That is a
bank extending credit on the strength of a chokepoint's endorsement, and it
worked for forty years before failing in 2023 for reasons that were about
interest rates rather than about technology.

Between the partnerships, the law firms, and the bank, a startup's entire
institutional environment was contained within a few square miles and was
constituted by people who knew each other. This is efficient, and the efficiency
is the barrier: an outsider is not merely unfunded, but unrepresented, unbanked,
and unintroduced.

## Who does not get through

The concentration is measurable and it is stark.

Studies of venture funding over the past several decades have consistently found
that the overwhelming majority of American venture capital goes to companies in
three metropolitan areas, that the share going to companies founded solely by
women has run in low single-digit percentages, and that the share going to Black
founders has been lower still. The partnerships making the decisions have had a
comparable composition.

The industry's explanation is pattern matching: partners fund founders who
resemble founders who have succeeded before, because base rates are the only
information available at the seed stage. That explanation is honest and it
describes a mechanism for reproducing an existing distribution indefinitely.

It is also, precisely, the sorting argument from Act II chapter 3 with the
biology removed and the vocabulary updated. A small group of credentialled
experts assesses human quality, ranks it, and allocates resources on the
ranking, and the ranking correlates with who was already advantaged.

Rock said he backed people rather than businesses. He was describing the
mechanism accurately. The question the chapter leaves is which people, and the
answer has been consistent for fifty years.
